answer: Sybil schemes assume attackers can pick who checks their work; the protocol removes that choice. Submissions close first; only then does the ledger draw reviewers from a large pool, seeded unpredictably. Authors never learn grader identities, so there is no counterparty to bribe and nothing to anchor a side payment to. Seats are terraced by track record, so a cluster wanting reliable self-grading must hold a visible share of every tier. It must buy seats as a builder buys timber: by the load, at published prices, no volume discount, held across epochs. Collusion costs more than honest work.
